content.text: Building a sourdough starter from flour and water only, without commercial yeast.

From day 2: keep 50 g of starter, feed 50 g whole-wheat flour + 50 g water every day (discard goes to the fridge)
Day 5: doubled in volume 6 hours after feeding
Day 7: doubles in 4–5 hours. The peak time has settled, so I will start baking with it
On a day when the room dropped to 22 °C it took 8 hours to double. Starter activity depends a lot on temperature
Water at 30 °C gets it going faster. Cold tap water set it back by half a day
On day 7 the starter peaks about 4 hours after feeding. Past the peak it sinks and turns sharply sour

doc.title: Oven temperature calibration

pages.title: Oven temperature calibration

content.text: The crust color kept coming out paler than the books describe, so I measured what the oven actually does.
Oven thermometer on the middle rack, center
Dial set to 200, 230 and 250 °C; after 20 minutes of preheating, read the thermometer
Every setting runs 14–16 °C below the dial. The offset is nearly constant
Opening the door drops it by almost 30 °C, and it takes 5 minutes to recover
When a recipe says 230 °C, set the dial to 245 °C
Preheat at least 20 minutes before loading. Keep the door open as briefly as possible
The "230 °C" in trials 1–7 was really about 215 °C. That explains the pale crust

doc.title: Reading notes - hydration and crumb structure

pages.title: Reading notes - hydration and crumb structure

content.text: Notes from a baking textbook and a flour mill's technical sheet on how hydration relates to crumb structure.
Hydration is the weight of water as a share of the flour weight. Typical ranges: 60–70% for sandwich loaves, 70–80% for hearth breads
More water makes the dough softer and more extensible, so the gas from fermentation grows into larger cells. That is why the crumb "opens"
Whether the dough can hold the water depends on the amount and quality of protein (gluten). Higher-protein flour absorbs more water, so at the same hydration the dough is tighter
Rule of thumb: a 1% difference in protein shifts absorption by about 2%. 75% on an 11% flour is roughly like 78–79% on a 12.5% flour
High-hydration dough builds gluten better through rests and folds than through kneading. An autolyse (flour and water rested first) also helps
Push hydration too far and the gluten network cannot support the water: the dough slackens, the loaf bakes flat, and the crumb ends up tighter, not more open
opened the crumb because the bread flour had enough protein
The failure with the lower-protein flour in
("spreads sideways, dense bottom") is exactly the slackening described here

doc.title: Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time

pages.title: Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time

content.text: Notes on sourdough fermentation temperature and time, from a book and from the baker who shared the starter with me.
Bulk fermentation is best at 24–27 °C. With 20% starter, expect the dough to double in 4–5 hours in that range
Each 1 °C rise speeds fermentation by roughly 10–15%. At 28 °C it runs about 30% faster than at 26 °C
Above 28 °C the acid-producing bacteria take over and the dough turns sour. Acid also weakens gluten, so an overblown dough collapses easily
Cold fermentation at 4–6 °C for 8–16 hours nearly stops the rise, but enzymes keep working and build aroma and sweetness. Cold dough is also easier to shape
Judge the end of fermentation by volume and the spring-back of a poke, not by the clock. Recipe times mean nothing once the temperature changes
(28 °C, 4 hours) collapsed because I let the clock, not the dough, decide. At 28 °C I should have stopped at 3 hours
(12 hours cold) matches the cold-fermentation effect described here

doc.title: Trial 7 - 75% hydration, lower-protein flour

pages.title: Trial 7 - 75% hydration, lower-protein flour

content.text: ("more water, more open crumb") with a different flour. Hydration kept at 75%, flour switched to an all-purpose type with 11.0% protein.
Even after four sets of folds the dough never tightened. It stayed sticky and never turned glossy
Out of the bowl after bulk, the dough spread sideways and could not hold a shape
Height 7.5 cm. Spread out and flat. Tight crumb with no large holes. The bottom is dense
Same 75% hydration as trial 3, opposite result

The crumb opened at 75% because the bread flour (12.5%) could hold that much water. With 11% protein there was too much water for the gluten network. "More water, more open crumb" holds only while the flour has enough protein. When changing flour, the hydration has to be chosen again for that flour.

content.text: A sourdough starter can be created using only whole‑wheat flour and water, with no commercial yeast added.
On day 1 the mixture was 50 g whole‑wheat flour and 50 g water at about 30 °C, loosely covered and kept on a shelf at 26 °C.
From day 2 onward 50 g of the starter was retained and fed daily with 50 g whole‑wheat flour and 50 g water; the discarded portion was stored in the refrigerator.
By day 3 a sour smell and tiny bubbles were observed.
On day 5 the starter doubled in volume six hours after feeding.
On day 7 the starter doubled in four to five hours after feeding, and the peak time had stabilized, indicating readiness for baking.
When the ambient temperature dropped to 22 °C, the doubling time increased to eight hours, showing that starter activity depends strongly on temperature.
Using water at 30 °C accelerated activity, whereas cold tap water delayed it by about half a day.
On day 7 the starter peaked approximately four hours after feeding; after the peak it sank and became sharply sour.

Higher hydration only opens the crumb when the flour provides sufficient protein; with all‑purpose flour at 75 % hydration the crumb was spread out and flat, unlike the open crumb seen with higher‑protein bread flour at the same hydration.
The dough’s ability to hold water depends on the amount and quality of protein; higher‑protein flour absorbs more water, so at the same hydration the dough is tighter

content.text: Fermenting at 28 °C for 4 h resulted in over‑fermentation, causing the loaf’s centre to sink.

The dough volume more than doubled within 3 h and was over‑blown with large surface bubbles by 4 h.
The dough showed little tension during shaping and slumped, indicating over‑fermentation.
Raising the fermentation temperature necessitates shortening the fermentation time.
A cold fermentation of 12 h produced a rise comparable to the high‑hydration trial and yielded better flavor.
A cold, long fermentation improves flavor.
Cold, long fermentation gave the same rise as trial 3 while improving flavor and aroma, and it suits a weekday schedule of mixing in the evening and baking in the morning.
A bulk fermentation of 2 h at 26 °C followed by 12 h at 4 °C, then a final proof of 2 h at 26 °C was used in the cold, long trial.
The cold dough was easy to handle and shaped cleanly.
Final proof started slowly but reached the rim of the tin in 2 h.
The loaf reached a height of 11 cm with an open crumb and more evenly sized holes.
The flavor was described as wheat sweetness, mild acidity, and deeper aroma, and the bread remained moist the next day.
The trial used 75 % hydration (225 g water to 300 g bread flour, 12.5 % protein).
Stretch‑and‑fold was performed four times at 30‑minute intervals, making the dough glossy and tightening it after the third fold.
During bulk fermentation at 26 °C for 4 h the dough volume doubled.
The loaf baked to 11 cm height with a beautifully open crumb, large holes, thin cell walls, deep colour and a crisp crust.
The trial was judged the best so far, supporting the reading that more water yields a more open crumb.
Bulk fermentation at 26 °C for 4 h increased dough volume to about 1.8 × the original, higher than the 1.6 × increase observed in trial 1.

The baseline loaf at 65 % hydration yielded a 9.5 cm-high loaf with a fine, even crumb that was slightly tight, moist but heavy, and toasted with a good bite; the dough was cohesive and easy to handle.
Bulk fermentation lasted 4 h at 26 °C with two folds, followed by a final proof of 2 h at 26 °C.
The starter was initiated with 30 °C water and kept at 26 °C ambient temperature.
By day 3 the starter produced a sour smell and tiny bubbles.
At 26 °C the starter doubled in volume 6 h after feeding on day 5.
By day 7 the same 26 °C starter doubled in 4–5 h after feeding, establishing a stable peak time.
When ambient temperature fell to 22 °C the doubling time lengthened to about 8 h.
Using water at 30 °C accelerated starter activity compared with cooler water.
Feeding with cold tap water delayed starter development by roughly half a day.
On day 7 the starter reached its peak approximately 4 h after feeding, after which it sank and became sharply sour.
Bulk fermentation is optimal at 24–27 °C; with 20 % starter the dough typically doubles in 4–5 h.
Each 1 °C increase in temperature accelerates fermentation by roughly 10–15 %, so at 28 °C the process runs about 30 % faster than at 26 °C.
Above 28 °C acid‑producing bacteria dominate, making the dough sour and weakening gluten, which causes over‑blown dough to collapse easily.
At 28 °C the dough should be stopped after about 3 h to prevent collapse.
Cold fermentation at 4–6 °C for 8–16 h nearly stops the rise, while enzymes continue to develop aroma and sweetness.
Fermentation should be judged by dough volume and the spring‑back of a poke rather than by elapsed time.
The improved flavor observed in the 12 h cold trial aligns with the cold‑fermentation effect described.
One trial reported the dough volume doubled during bulk fermentation at 26 °C for 4 h, whereas another reported an increase to about 1.8 × under the same conditions.

messages.content: If I use 30% whole wheat, what hydration should I go for? Base it on my trials so far

Based on the data you’ve collected, a 30 % whole‑wheat inclusion needs a higher fluid level than the 75 % you used in Trial 6.

| Trial | Flour mix (30 % whole‑wheat) | Hydration used | Observed result |
|------|-----------------------------|----------------|-----------------|
| 6 (a) | 12.5 % bread flour + 30 % whole‑wheat (210 g + 90 g) | 75 % (225 g water) | Dough was stiff, bran soaked water, folds tore the dough, and the crumb was tight with small holes. |
| 6 (b) | Same mix | **≈ 80 %** (recommended) | Lesson note says “hydration probably needs to go up to about 80 %” to regain extensibility and crumb openness. | 

**Why raise it to ~80 %?**

1. **Whole‑wheat absorbs more water** than pure bread flour, so the same absolute water amount yields a dryer, less‑elastic dough. This is reflected in your observation that the dough felt “stiff right after mixing” and “the bran seems to soak it up”[Source: "Trial 6 - replacing 30% with whole wheat"].  
2. Your own “Lesson and next” entry explicitly states that “hydration probably needs to go up to about 80 %” when the flour contains 30 % whole wheat[Source: "Trial 6 - replacing 30% with whole wheat"].  
3. The knowledge base records the same guideline: “Increasing hydration to ~80 % may be needed with 30 % whole wheat” — a finding derived from your experiments and broader practice — [Source: "Increasing hydration to ~80% may be needed with 30% whole wheat"].  
4. An atom in the schema notes that “Whole‑wheat flour demands higher hydration levels” — [Source: "Whole‑wheat flour demands higher hydration levels"].

**Practical recommendation**

- **Target hydration:** **78 %–80 %** (≈ 235–240 g water for a 300 g total flour batch).  
- **Why a range:** 78 % often restores workability without making the dough overly slack; 80 % matches the “about 80 %” you noted and should give the crumb the openness you saw with 75 % hydration on all‑bread‑flour loaves.  

**What to watch for**

- **Dough feel:** It should feel supple instead of stiff; the folds should stretch rather than tear.  
- **Crumb texture:** If the crumb still feels dense, you can push a little higher (up to 82 %) but keep an eye on gluten development (see the principle that “more water opens crumb only when flour protein is sufficient”).  

So, for a 30 % whole‑wheat formulation, aim for roughly **80 % hydration** (±2 %). This should balance the extra water demand of the whole‑wheat components while preserving the open crumb you’re after.

---

  - [Source: "Increasing hydration to ~80% may be needed with 30% whole wheat"]
  - [Source: "Whole‑wheat flour demands higher hydration levels"]
Trials 3 and 7 both used 75% hydration. Why did they come out opposite?

Both trials were run at the same **75 % hydration**, but the flour they used differed in protein content, and that changes how much water the dough can hold and how strong the gluten network will be.

| Trial | Flour type | Approx. protein | Result |
|-------|------------|----------------|--------|
| 3 | Bread flour (≈12.5 % protein) | High | Very open crumb, large holes |
| 7 | All‑purpose flour (≈11 % protein) | Lower | Dough spread, flat loaf, dense bottom |

**Why the opposite outcomes**

1. **Gluten strength matters** – Bread flour’s higher protein can develop a robust gluten network that tolerates the extra water, keeping the dough elastic enough to trap gas and produce an open crumb. [Source: "Trial 3 - 75% hydration, bread flour"] [Source: "Trial plan and log"]  

2. **Too much water for low‑protein flour slackens gluten** – With all‑purpose flour the same amount of water exceeds what the gluten matrix can support. The dough becomes overly slack, loses tension, and spreads out in the pan; the crumb stays tight and the loaf flattens. [Source: "Trial 7 - 75% hydration, lower-protein flour"] [Source: "All‑purpose flour at 75 % hydration spreads and flattens"]  

3. **The “more water → more open crumb” rule is conditional** – Your own note states that “more water, more open crumb holds only while the flour has enough protein” and that when the flour changes the hydration must be readjusted. [Source: "Trial 7 - 75% hydration, lower-protein flour"]  

4. **Insight from distilled knowledge** – An excess of water can actually make the crumb denser because it weakens gluten cohesion, which is exactly what happened with the lower‑protein flour. [Source: "Too much water makes the crumb denser"]  

So, the opposite results stem from **protein‑dependent water tolerance**: 75 % hydration is optimal for the higher‑protein bread flour, but it is too high for the lower‑protein all‑purpose flour, causing the dough to spread and the crumb to become dense. Adjusting the hydration downward (or using a higher‑protein flour) restores the balance and yields the expected open crumb.

messages.content: If I ferment at 28 °C, how long should it take?

At 28 °C the dough ferments noticeably faster than at the “standard” 24 – 27 °C range.  

* A 1 °C rise speeds fermentation by roughly 10–15 % per degree → the 2 °C increase from 26 °C to 28 °C makes the bulk rise about 30 % faster [Source: "Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time"].  
* In practice you see the dough double in volume after ≈ 3 h rather than the ≈ 4 h you’d expect at 26 °C [Source: "There is an optimal fermentation duration for each temperature"].  

So, if you keep the same starter proportion (≈ 20 % of flour weight) and other conditions unchanged, aim for **about 3 hours of bulk fermentation at 28 °C**, watching the dough’s volume and its “spring‑back” when gently pressed. If the dough has already doubled and feels loose, it’s time to stop; letting it run to 4 h typically leads to over‑fermentation, loss of dough tension and a collapsed crumb [Source: "Trial 4 - fermenting at 28 C"][Source: "Reading notes - fermentation temperature and time"].
